# Setup

First, let's load the two packages we need for this class, which are tidycensus and tidyverse.

```{r setup, message = F, warning=F}
library(tidyverse)
library(tidycensus)
```

# Agenda

- Discuss APIs in modern data architecture
- Introduce the Decennial Census
- Introduce the American Community Survey (ACS)
- Differences between Decennial Census and ACS
- In-class activity

# Concepts for this Class

## APIs

- API = Application Programming Interface
- Software that sits on top of another system and can be used to interact with it.
- Most modern systems have one or more APIs, and each API often has multiple “endpoints” that can perform various tasks with the data.
- APIs can be invoked directly from your code, or indirectly via functions that are included with certain R packages (like tidycensus!)

## API Key

You need a Census API key for using `tidycensus`: <http://api.census.gov/data/key_signup.html>. You can then store this key in RStudio using `tidycensus::census_api_key("",install=TRUE)`

## tidycensus

**tidycensus** is an R package that allows users to interface with the US Census Bureau’s APIs and return tidyverse-ready data frames for the decennial and ACS datasets.

It is created and maintained by **Kyle Walker**, a professor at Texas Christian University (TCU).

Dr. Walker wrote the [Analyzing US Census Data](https://walker-data.com/census-r/index.html){target="_blank"} textbook we are using for this portion of the course.

## The Decennial Census

- Conducted every 10 years.
- The last three were conducted in 2020, 2010, and 2000.
- Goal: to provide a reliable **point-in-time** estimate of the official U.S. population to Congress.
- Used for apportionment of congressional seats and distribution of federal funds.

## American Community Survey (ACS)

- An ongoing survey conducted every year.
- Goal: to provide **period estimates (1-year, 3-year, and 5-year)** of the U.S. population.
- Collects more detailed data, including age, race, income, commute time to work, home ownership, and other important community aspects.

:::

## Getting ACS data (basic)

```{r}
get_decennial(year = 2010,
              geography = "state", 
              variables = "P001001")
```

1.  Call the `get_acs()` function
2.  Specify the year
3.  Specify the **dataset** you want
4.  Specify the geography level
5.  Specify the variable(s)

::: callout-note
We'll take a closer look at this in our next class!
:::

## Decennial vs. ACS

- **Frequency**: Decennial is every 10 years, ACS is annually.
- **Data granularity**: Decennial provides a complete enumeration, ACS provides estimates based on a sample.
- **Detail level**: The decennial census is focused on counting the total population, whereas the ACS provides more detailed socioeconomic data.

## Census resources

- The [Walker textbook](https://walker-data.com/census-r/index.html){target="_blank"} we're reading is a useful guide for understanding how to get valuable data out of the tidycensus package.
- The website [Social Explorer](https://www.socialexplorer.com/explore-maps){target="_blank"} is valuable for exploring census data, including data dictionaries that contain variable definitions, and an interactive "report builder" that lets you build your own data tables.
- **Use these two resources together to ace this part of the class!**

### Part 3

Big question: **How do we know what variable codes to look for?**

U.S. census data is **massive** and byzantine in its structure, so finding the right variable and what it means can be a complicated affair.

Luckily, there are a few methods you can use:

#### load_variables

The most direct way to get variable codes and descriptions into RStudio is by calling the `load_variables()` function, which is part of the tidycensus package. Our next lesson focuses very heavily on this method.

```{r}

```

#### census.gov

The census.gov website has an interactive data portal where you can explore their tables. Link: [Census Bureau Tables](https://data.census.gov/table){target="_blank"}

This interface gives you some capability to explore the available tables and their variables.

When searching for variables for the 2020 decennial census, I recommend you stick to the **Demographic and Housing Characteristics (DHC) dataset** because this has the most data. Again, this is a huge amount of data to work with, but the DHC dataset contains the most possibilities for your final project and other work you might want to do with census data.

Another option under census.gov is their [developer portal](https://www.census.gov/data/developers.html){target="_blank"}, which has a lot of links to documentation that can be helpful for finding variables.

Here are their [decennial datasets](https://www.census.gov/data/developers/data-sets/decennial-census.html){target="_blank"}

And here are their [ACS 5-year datsets](https://www.census.gov/data/developers/data-sets/acs-5year.html){target="_blank"}

These dataset pages link to helpful tables you can browse with codes and descriptions of their variables, such as: - [2020 decennial DHC variables](https://api.census.gov/data/2020/dec/dhc/variables.html){target="_blank"} - [2023 ACS 5-year variables](https://api.census.gov/data/2023/acs/acs5/variables.html){target="_blank"}

::: callout-caution
These tables are massive, so use your browser's built-in search features to do keyword searches for specific words and terms.
:::

#### Social Explorer

[Social Explorer's data library](https://www.socialexplorer.com/data-library){target="_blank"} has a streamlined interface for interacting with census tables from both the ACS and the decennial census. They don't have the entire 2020 decennial census yet (they seem to be lacking the DHC dataset), but they have really good tools for exploring recent ACS datasets.

The trick with the Social Explorer is that they use their own proprietary variable codes for census data, so when you find a variable you like and want to analyze with tidycensus, you need to drill down into the Social Explorer's data dictionary to find the equivalent census variable code.
